items.title: iPhone Duo sells out moments after pre-orders begin
items.content_html:
As expected, Apple's iPhone Duo has seen shipping slip back in most configurations instantly.

Pre-orders for the iPhone Duo began at 8 A.M. Eastern and as with most new iPhones — but not all — the stocks sold out rapidly. With the first moments, shipping dates slipped back to November 16, and then to November 23, for all configurations.

Apple never states how many devices it has made ready for sale on day one, but the shipping dates normally provide a clue as to whether a model is a hit.

In this case, that's less apparent than usual because there is another factor. Alongside demand from early buyers, it's believed that Apple has fewer of the iPhone Duo manufactured than normal.

That could be because of the many reports of delays in manufacturing over such a complex new design. But there is also the fact that this is a new design and so demand may have proven harder to estimate.

Then, too, the iPhone Duo is the most expensive iPhone ever made. It's also launching at a time when the global chip shortage has driven all technology prices higher.

You will still be able to place an order for the iPhone Duo, you just won't get it when the first shipments begin on October 23. However, that same date is when the iPhone Duo will be in stores, and those stores will have at least some stocks.

items.title: Apple Maps Detailed City Experience comes to Austin, Texas ahead of F1 Grand Prix
items.content_html:
Apple's Pixar-like Maps upgrade has arrived in Austin, Texas to help F1 racegoers get around in style, plus Circuit of the Americas has some custom details in time for the Grand Prix.

Apple Maps has been updating F1 tracks around the world as races occur there. It is a part of promoting Apple's ownership of the US streaming rights of F1 using its various services.

The latest track to get special immersive details is the Circuit of the Americas in Austin, Texas. Apple also took the time to update the rest of Austin with its Detailed City Experience.

Apple has been rolling out the Detailed City Experience to major locations in the United States since 2021. It's been a slow process, but has always been worth the wait when custom art and Pixar-like graphics are added to represent a city.

Visit the racetrack in Apple Maps and you'll see custom art for the track and various nearby attractions, like COTALAND Theme Park. The updated maps aren't just pretty to look at, Apple has worked to ensure information about grandstands, entry gates, rideshare locations, pedestrian walkways, and more are available in the app.

There is also a new Apple Maps Guide on country music singer Dylan Gossett's Austin Spots. Explore the highlighted businesses with their custom 3D artwork among highly detailed streets and foliage.

See Circuit of the Americas in detail ahead of the F1 Grand Prix

New 3D landmarks include the Apple Domain Northside, Black's Barbecue, LBJ Presidential Library, and the Paramount Theater. Notice small details, like birds flying over the Ann W. Richards Congress Avenue Bridge.

The F1 Grand Prix at Circuit of the Americas takes place on October 25 at 2:50 p.m. EST. It can be viewed in the Apple TV app.

items.title: Elevation Lab pulls its AirTag Silencer over stalking concerns, issues apology
items.content_html:
Elevation Lab has withdrawn its AirTag Silencer and apologized after acknowledging that permanently disabling the tracker's speaker could help people track victims without their knowledge.

Elevation Lab recently released a tool dubbed the AirTag Silencer. To use it, an AirTag owner could remove the battery, insert the AirTag into a jig, and use a hammer to drive a pin directly into the AirTag's speaker.

The pin would permanently silence the speaker without damaging any of the other components within the tracker. The creators say the tool was created to prevent thieves from uncovering the AirTag before the stolen item could be located.

AppleInsider refused to cover the AirTag Silencer when it launched. We believe this product, while it may have been created with good intentions, would enable users to track victims without their knowledge.

It's also a good time to remind you that AirTag is not an anti-theft device; it is an item tracker. While it may incidentally help recover stolen items, Apple clearly states that it's for misplaced items.

Elevation Lab has since removed the item and issued an apology:

Since its inception, many cases of unwanted tracking have plagued Apple's tiny tracker. In September 2026, a woman claimed a former partner used an AirTag to track her, and that the AirTag never warned her she was being tracked.

A month prior, two women in Detroit alleged they were tracked by their former partners using AirTag, but had never received an alert.

Another lawsuit from 2022 attempted to create a class-action challenge against Apple, accusing the anti-stalking measures of being inadequate and permitting unlawful tracking.

While that suit was given permission to proceed in 2024, it lost class-action certification in March 2026. This led to plaintiffs refiling in May.

items.title: That five-year-old Apple TV 4K is getting Siri AI
items.content_html:
Apple's new Siri AI is coming to Apple TV 4K models dating back to 2021, giving existing owners the upgraded assistant without a $299 hardware purchase.

The new Siri AI beta will work on Apple TV 4K models dating back to the second generation, so owners won't need to buy the latest hardware to use the upgraded assistant.

The feature brings a more conversational version of Siri to the television, with natural-language searches, follow-up questions, and personalized recommendations. It also introduces a full-screen interface for exploring movies and TV shows.

Users can ask Siri which Apple TV shows won Emmy Awards, request recommendations, or ask questions about something they're watching. Responses appear in a compact overlay during playback, allowing viewers to continue watching without interrupting the screen.

Siri AI will be available in beta with tvOS 27.2 on Apple TV 4K (2nd generation or later). The feature requires the home's owner to have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPhone or iPad running the latest software, with Siri AI enabled in a supported language.

With a compatible device paired, Siri can also access personal context to handle requests such as playing a show recommended by someone in a message.

At launch, Siri AI will support English in eight countries, including the United States, Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand, Singapore, South Africa, and the United Kingdom.

The fourth-generation Apple TV 4K adds three far-field microphones for hands-free Siri commands, even while audio is playing. Older Apple TV 4K models also support Siri AI, but lack the new model's built-in microphones.

items.title: Don't let iPhone Duo go unprotected, these are the best case options so far
items.content_html:
The best iPhone Duo cases protect Apple's foldable without getting in the way of its hinge, with options ranging from slim MagSafe shells to rugged designs with reinforced protection.

A conventional iPhone case only needs to fit around one solid body. The iPhone Duo introduces another consideration with its folding hinge, which needs to move freely while the rest of the phone stays protected.

Case makers have approached the challenge in different ways. Some favor thin shells that preserve the phone's original dimensions, while others offer dedicated hinge protection, integrated stands, and reinforced corners.

We've rounded up seven iPhone Duo cases from Spigen, Torras, ESR, and OtterBox, with options ranging from lightweight everyday protection to more rugged designs.

The Spigen Nano Pop MagFit is a good starting point for anyone who wants a protective iPhone Duo case without spending a fortune. Its two-tone design gives the phone some personality, while the textured sides make the device easier to grip when folded or unfolded.

Buy Spigen Nano Pop MagFit

Spigen combines a rigid polycarbonate interior with a flexible TPU exterior, using its Air Cushion technology to help absorb impacts around the corners. A laser-embossed dot pattern runs along the sides, adding texture without requiring a bulky rubber coating.

The case also includes N52 magnets for MagSafe chargers, mounts, and other magnetic accessories. Its open hinge design keeps things simple and relatively slim, although it leaves the folding mechanism more exposed than cases with a dedicated hinge guard.

At $26.99 on Amazon, the Nano Pop is the least expensive case in our roundup. It's a sensible choice if you prefer a lightweight shell and don't need extensive hinge coverage.

Watching videos on the iPhone Duo's unfolded display is more convenient when you don't have to find something to prop it against. The Torras Q3 Spin solves that problem with a built-in magnetic stand that rotates 360 degrees, supporting portrait and landscape viewing.

Buy Torras Q3 Spin

The stand works with the phone folded, partially opened, or fully unfolded, making it useful for video calls and other hands-free activities. It also folds against the back when you're finished, so you won't need to carry a separate stand.

Torras hasn't neglected protection, either. The Q3 Spin covers the front and back of the iPhone Duo, with a dedicated hinge guard that moves with the folding mechanism. The company says the hinge design has survived more than 30,000 folding cycles in laboratory testing.

Reinforced corners, raised camera edges, and a textured grip add protection around the rest of the phone. Torras also includes a tempered glass screen protector, and the case supports magnetic accessories and wireless charging.

The Torras Q3 Spin costs $69.99 on Amazon. It's particularly appealing if you want hinge coverage and regularly use the larger display for entertainment or work.

Not everyone wants to wrap a foldable phone in a thick protective shell. The Torras Q3 VegSkin takes a more understated approach, combining a leather-style finish with a slim rear case and a rotating magnetic stand.

Its soft-touch exterior offers a different feel from conventional plastic cases, with a textured finish that looks more at home in an office than a rugged workshop. The independent rear shell also avoids adding another protective layer across the entire front of the phone, helping preserve the iPhone Duo's slimmer profile.

Buy Torras Q3 VegSkin

There's still some protection around vulnerable areas. Torras includes raised edges, a hinge guard, and a microfiber lining to reduce scratches where the case meets the phone. A dedicated Camera Control button cover provides access to camera functions without leaving the control exposed.

The rotating stand supports both portrait and landscape viewing, while 38 N56 magnets provide compatibility with MagSafe chargers, wallets, and mounts. The stand folds flat against the rear shell when it isn't needed.

The Torras Q3 VegSkin sells for $79.99 on Amazon. It's worth considering if you want a leather-like finish and an integrated stand, but prefer something less substantial than the Q3 Spin.

The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case offers a useful compromise between showing off the iPhone Duo and keeping it protected. Its clear-black design leaves part of the phone visible, while a reinforced frame surrounds the edges and folding mechanism.

Buy ESR Classic Hybrid case

ESR uses a polycarbonate and acrylic back with a flexible TPU frame to absorb everyday impacts. The company's Air Guard corners provide additional cushioning, and ESR advertises drop protection from heights of up to eight feet. Raised edges and reinforced hinge coverage provide another layer of protection around exposed surfaces.

One of the more practical features is the integrated Flex Stand. It rotates and folds through 180 degrees, giving you different ways to position the iPhone Duo for watching videos, reading, or taking calls. The stand works with the phone open or folded and can cover the camera lenses when closed.

ESR has also kept the back relatively thin at 1.5 mm, despite the extra features. The case supports magnetic accessories, with ESR advertising 1,500 grams of magnetic holding force and compatibility with Qi2 25W charging.

The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case with Flex Stand costs $42.99 through ESR. It's one of the more affordable ways to get a folding stand, magnetic compatibility, and added hinge coverage in the same case.

ESR's Atelier Silicone Leather Magnetic Case gives the iPhone Duo a softer, more refined finish without abandoning the conveniences of a modern protective case. Its silicone leather exterior has a smooth texture, and an oleophobic coating helps resist fingerprints and everyday stains.

Buy ESR Atelier case

The design also includes a microfiber lining, raised edges, and a flexible TPU frame to protect against scratches and minor impacts. ESR advertises drop protection from heights of up to 3.6 feet, along with additional coverage around the hinge.

Like the Classic Hybrid, the Atelier includes a Flex Stand that rotates and folds through 180 degrees. You can use it to position the phone for hands-free viewing while it's open or folded, without attaching another accessory.

Built-in magnets maintain compatibility with MagSafe chargers and accessories, with ESR rating their holding force at 1,400 grams. The combination of magnetic charging, hinge protection, and a leather-like exterior makes the Atelier a more polished alternative to a conventional plastic case.

The ESR Atelier Silicone Leather Magnetic Case with Flex Stand is priced at $59.99 through ESR. It's a good fit if you prefer a softer exterior but still want the convenience of an integrated stand.

The OtterBox Lumen Series is designed for people who want to keep the iPhone Duo looking like an iPhone Duo. Its slim, two-piece construction follows the phone's contours and accommodates the folding hinge without surrounding it with a bulky protective cover.

Buy OtterBox Lumen case

OtterBox offers clear and translucent finishes, including Black Mist and Tortoise, so the phone's appearance remains part of the design. The scratch-resistant exterior helps maintain that look, while raised edges provide clearance around the screen and camera when the device rests on a flat surface.

Despite its slim construction, the Lumen isn't purely decorative. OtterBox says it has been tested to three times the military drop standard MIL-STD-810G 516.6. The case also provides custom-fit coverage around the camera area, along with built-in magnets for MagSafe chargers and accessories.

You'll retain full access to Camera Control, and integrated anchor points allow you to attach straps or charms. The latter could be particularly useful if you're concerned about dropping a phone that unfolds into a larger device.

The OtterBox Lumen Series is listed for $49.99 through OtterBox, with units coming soon. Best Buy also sells the case, but for $69.99. It's a compelling option if you want a clear case with drop protection while keeping added bulk to a minimum.

The OtterBox Defender Series Pro XT takes the opposite approach from the Lumen, putting more emphasis on protecting the iPhone Duo's vulnerable areas. Its rugged construction includes a dedicated hinge guard, reinforced edges, and covers that help keep dirt and dust out of the ports.

The hinge guard moves with the phone and lies flat when the iPhone Duo is unfolded. OtterBox has also designed the hinge area to provide additional gripping space when the phone is open, which could make the larger device easier to hold securely.

Buy OtterBox Defender Pro XT

The Defender Series Pro XT combines polycarbonate and thermoplastic elastomer materials with textured edges that provide extra grip. According to OtterBox, the case has been tested to four times the military drop standard MIL-STD-810G 516.6. Built-in magnets also allow wireless charging without removing the case.

All that protection adds some weight and thickness, so the Defender won't appeal to everyone. However, the extra coverage makes sense if you regularly use your phone outdoors, work in demanding environments, or simply want more protection around the folding hardware.

The OtterBox Defender Series Pro XT is listed for $89.99 through Best Buy and OtterBox.com. It's the most rugged-focused option in our roundup and the one to consider if protecting the hinge is your main concern.

Picking a case for the iPhone Duo involves a few trade-offs you don't usually encounter with a conventional iPhone. A slimmer shell preserves the phone's original feel, but it may leave more of the hinge exposed. A more protective design covers additional surfaces, although that generally means carrying a thicker device.

Integrated stands are worth considering, too. The Torras and ESR cases make it easier to take advantage of the Duo's unfolded display without finding something to lean the phone against. If neither of the featured ESR models suits your needs, the company also has additional options in its iPhone Duo collection.

All seven cases offer magnetic accessory compatibility, but they differ in materials, grip, hinge coverage, and overall bulk. The right choice depends on whether you want to preserve the Duo's thin profile, get more use from its larger display, or provide additional protection for the folding hardware.

items.title: Where Apple focused engineering so the iPhone Duo could have desktop-like performance
items.content_html:
To make the iPhone Duo as thin as it is, Apple needed to make a lot of design choices to fend off heat. Here's what they did, how they did it, and where in the device the innovations live.

Folding devices like the iPhone Duo often raise engineering challenges due to their unique design. However, solving problems like making as thin a smartphone as possible can lead to the creation of others, such as keeping it cool.

In an interview with PCMag, Apple's VP of silicon engineering Dan Murray and senior manager of thermal product design Banafsheh Barabadi discussed how Apple fixed heat issues in the iPhone Duo.

The discussion first covered the "M-Class-inspired packaging design" of the A20 Pro, referring to a change from the package-on-package (POP) process Apple previously used. Rather than a vertical stack for the system-on-chip (SOC) and the memory, Apple moved the DRAM module next to the processor.

The "M-Class" stems from the idea that a notebook like a MacBook Pro has a lot more internal space to play with than a smartphone. The memory can easily be placed separately from the processor, rather than requiring it to be stacked to save space.

The use of a wafer-level multichip module (WMCM) packaging technique helped spread out the heat instead of confining it to one place. The location also meant that the memory still had fast communications with the chip itself.

While Apple has used vapor chambers in the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max, Apple redesigned the idea for the A20 Pro used in the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. The chassis were also redesigned to work better with the thermal technique.

There are four pillars to heat management, with the first being direct silicon access. The shifting of the DRAM from the vertical stack helped this, since heat from the silicon has a more direct path to the vapor chamber.

"Metal over foam" is the second pillar, creating a direct thermal and mechanically compliant coupling between the vapor chamber and chip. "It took us months of development to get the material properties exactly right," the engineers explained.

The technique was first spotted during a teardown of the iPhone 18 Pro, described at the time as "thermal chainmail" inside a pad.

The third is the vapor chamber, which now as three times the surface area as the previous version, along with more de-ionized water. The chamber also serves as the "central structural plane for the device," said Barabadi, with the battery and logic board mounted directly to it.

Lastly, the fourth is a new layer on the back of the foldable display to keep it sturdy. It's described as a "nanotube copper display metal plate material" that provides mechanical strength for the display.

The copper plate also has a high level of thermal conductivity, combined with a high-conductivity graphite layer. The result is that heat is spread more evenly across the display, reducing hotspots.

"When we combine these four pillars together, it meaningfully improves the thermal performance across every metric," said Barabadi.

The thermal antics aren't just limited to the main body of the iPhone Duo. The all-important hinge does its part too.

Since the iPhone Duo has two halves, connected by a hinge, the two thin halves become one much thicker device when closed. For heat management, this is a problem, because the vapor chamber in the iPhone Duo floats in the middle.

To thermally connect the two halves of the chamber, there's a flexible graphite pipe going through the hinge. This transfers heat between the two sides, balancing the temperature throughout the devices.

It also considerably increased the surface area used for heat dissipation.

To Apple, the part needed to be worked on by both the thermal and mechanical teams. All due to being a flexible material that needed to survive thousands of hinge activations throughout the iPhone Duo's lifespan.

items.title: Unlikely Apple & Meta team-up brings powerful & local AI to Mac Studio
items.content_html:
Meta worked with Apple to bring its massive Muse Spark Open AI model to M5 Ultra Mac Studios, letting developers run advanced AI locally instead of relying on cloud servers.

Announced on October 15, Muse Spark Open is an open-weight AI model designed for coding, software engineering, and tasks that require multiple steps. Meta developed the model with 816 billion parameters, although only 42 billion are active during processing.

Running the model requires at least two M5 Ultra Mac Studios with 512GB of unified memory each, or four machines configured with 256GB each, using hardware introduced in Apple's recent Mac Studio refresh. The four-machine configuration is available now, but Apple's 512GB option isn't expected to ship until late October.

The collaboration takes advantage of Apple's unified memory architecture, which allows the CPU and GPU to access the same memory pool. The M5 Ultra provides up to 512GB of unified memory and 1.2TB/s of memory bandwidth.

Even that much memory isn't enough for Muse Spark Open on a single machine. According to Apple's research, the model's compressed weights occupy approximately 493GB before accounting for the additional memory required during processing.

The open-source MLX framework handles the Meta model's execution by distributing the workload across multiple Macs. The machines communicate using Thunderbolt 5 and remote direct memory access, or RDMA, which allows them to exchange data with less CPU involvement.

Apple updated MLX to support Muse Spark Open, improving communication between connected Macs and adding support for the M5 Ultra's GPU Neural Accelerators. The framework can split the model across multiple computers or distribute calculations between them to speed up processing.

In Apple's benchmarks, four M5 Ultra Mac Studios generated more than 36 tokens per second with an 8,192-token context. Actual performance depends on the workload and context length, but the results show the model can deliver responses at a practical speed.

Meta demonstrated the model handling several complex workflows entirely on local hardware. Using its Muse Code development tool, the model modified Ice Cubes, an open-source Mastodon client for iOS, fixing bugs, adding features, and completing a build.

Another demonstration showed Muse Spark Open controlling DaVinci Resolve to review video footage, identify useful segments, and crop them into vertical clips. The demonstrations show the model completing specific tasks but don't establish how reliably Muse Spark Open performs across other workflows.

The biggest obstacle is the hardware requirement. The M5 Ultra Mac Studio starts at $5,499, but the memory configurations needed for Muse Spark Open push a multi-machine setup into the tens of thousands of dollars.

The hardware costs make Muse Spark Open better suited to professional development and research than occasional use. Developers with occasional needs may prefer hosted services, while frequent users can avoid cloud usage fees.

The collaboration is also notable given the companies' history. Apple and Meta have clashed over privacy, advertising restrictions, and platform control, but their interests align when it comes to running advanced AI models on Apple's hardware.

For Apple, Muse Spark Open demonstrates the Mac Studio's AI capabilities. For Meta, the partnership offers another way to run its models without relying on cloud infrastructure or dedicated GPU servers.

Muse Spark Open is available through Hugging Face, with support for additional hardware from AMD, Intel, and Nvidia. Developers without the necessary equipment can also access the model through hosted API providers.

Open-weight availability doesn't mean the model is unrestricted. Meta distributes Muse Spark Open under its own license, which permits many uses without charge but includes commercial limitations.

items.title: iPhone Duo preorders have started
items.content_html:
We have confirmed that Apple's first foldable iPhone is now available to preorder, with launch-day delivery dates expected to slip quickly.

The Apple Store is back online, with preorders for the iPhone Duo now officially open. Apple once again is using a queue system and will open the order page when it has reached your spot in the queue.

As it's done before, Apple opened a preorder configuration option ahead of the launch, allowing buyers to select their preferred configuration and payment method. Those selections help speed up checkout when preorders are live.

iPhone Duo preorders began at 5:00 a.m. Pacific, or 8:00 a.m. Eastern. Store access will vary as Apple's global content delivery system spins up in data centers across the world, and the Apple Store app comes back online.

Some buyers may see the store before others, depending on how and where they access it. We don't run a piece like this until we can confirm that iPhone Duo preorders are live, with the aforementioned queue.

If you don't see the store, try switching between the website and the Apple Store app.

Delivery dates for the iPhone Duo will begin slipping as preorder demand builds. Popular configurations can quickly move beyond launch-day delivery.

The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 with 256GB of storage. A maxed out iPhone Duo with 2TB of storage will cost $3,199 before any trade-in or carrier deals.

items.title: Just about all of 'No Man's Sky' is coming to iPhone and iPad
items.content_html:
Hello Games is bringing "No Man's Sky" to iOS and iPadOS, with preorders for the mobile version starting ahead of its October 28 release date.

"No Man's Sky" is a game that has been around since August 2016, and only became available on Mac as recently as June 2023. Now, over a decade after the initial release, "No Man's Sky" is finally landing on iPhone and iPad.

The sci-fi adventure game is set in a procedurally-generated universe, filled with countless solar systems, planets, and space stations. Starting on the outer rim, players can explore unique planets, build bases, and upgrade their ships as they try to reach the center of the universe.

While it's finally traversing the software landscape to iOS and iPadOS, the release isn't a cut-down version designed for mobile users. Instead, it's the same full universe that players on other platforms already enjoy.

That includes recent updates such as COSMOS, and the 2025 Voyagers update that introduced customizable big-rig starships.

No Man's Sky on an iPad, with interface - Image Credit: Hello Games

However, there are some small concessions, in line with the Nintendo Switch version of the game, following player feedback. There wasn't multiplayer or "settlements" on Day 1, which will be the same on iOS from launch.

It also introduces a new set of touch controls to work with the mobile displays. Players can still elect to play with controllers, mouse and keyboard on an iPad, and casting to a television for big-screen gaming.

As an ambitious game, it does take a hefty amount of storage space, but not as much as you'd think. The developers say that installation is less than 5 gigabytes, despite the sheer scale of the in-game universe.

While it is a ten-year-old game, there were inklings of a move to iPhone and iPad a few years ago.

The WWDC 2022 launch of the Metal 3 API and the MetalFX framework was accompanied by discussion of how it would be used to improve the performance of "No Man's Sky" on Mac. MetalFX is used to manage upscaling, as well as drawing extra frames to improve frame rates.

In a June 2023 interview with AppleInsider for the Mac version's launch, Hello Games CEO Sean Murray talked about how Mac and iOS was something the studio always considers. The move to Metal had taken almost two years at that point, with Apple assisting one year into the effort.

Murray was enthusiastic about the App Store and its reach to new users who may not have heard of his company's games.

However, developing for Mac and iPad are very different tasks. "Suddenly you have to consider a new user interface, battery life, things like that," Murry said, adding that you have to consider how that audience "like to play their games."

At the time, he didn't directly say a mobile edition of "No Man's Sky" was on the way, but hinted at it.

Moving to Vulkan enabled Hello Games to work with Metal, and likewise the move to VR opened up the possibility of developing for the Nintendo Switch and mobile hardware. Murray ended the thought by saying he was excited to see where Metal might lead to, and that it was "just our next step in a longer journey."

The game is available to preorder from the App Store on Monday, October 12 as part of Apple's App Store Indie Games Week. The full release is on October 28, with a free-to-try element at launch.

Unlocking the full game will cost $19.99.

items.title: Apple inadvertently reveals new iPad mini model exists
items.content_html:
An iPad mini refresh with an OLED panel is expected at the end of October, but it seems Apple may have leaked its existence early thanks to a French Regulatory website.

There may be a lot of rumors and anonymous tipsters out there trying to reveal Apple's upcoming products, but sometimes the leaks come from within the company itself. An iPad mini was almost certain to arrive before the end of 2026, but now Apple seems to have confirmed it.

A French Apple regulatory webpage was first discovered by MacRumors containing an iPad identifier that didn't belong to any existing model. The listing is for a Smart Folio for iPad mini belonging to model A3632.

Apple's "Identify your iPad model" webpage doesn't contain that model number. If you've ever paid much attention to these model numbers, they don't appear to conform to any real rhyme or reason.

The current iPad mini with A17 Pro has an A2993 model number, while iPhone 17e is the closest to this new iPad mini's sequence with an A3634 number. A leak of several model numbers in August didn't contain this model number.

All this leak does is confirm what rumors have been saying for months. Expect the new iPad mini with increased water resistance and an OLED display to be revealed during Apple's expected October 28 event.

items.title: Online Apple Store goes down ahead of iPhone Duo pre-orders
items.content_html:
The online version of the Apple Store has gone temporarily offline, all in preparation for the opening of pre-orders for the iPhone Duo, Apple's first-ever foldable iPhone.

Whenever Apple makes a small but important change to the online Apple Store, it takes the site down first. It's theatrics more than site maintenance, but it's obviously worth it to Apple despite how until it's back up, no one can buy anything in the online store. As usual, that has just happened, ahead of Apple opening up pre-orders for the iPhone Duo.

Visitors to the digital storefront are currently greeted by the traditional combination of an Apple logo and a "We love that early energy" message. There's also a promise that Apple's site will "see you soon."

The changes this time are solely around the iPhone Duo. Announced at the September 9, 2026 "Surprise and Shine" event, it has taken until now for Apple to begin accepting pre-orders for the device.

That means the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, HomePod mini 2, updated Apple TV 4K, and even the HomeView, have all been launched while we waited to buy an iPhone Duo.

The long gap may be because of regularly reported production issues with making the iPhone Duo in sufficient quantities. And it's perhaps because of this long delay that Apple launched a special "Get Ready" ability to pre-pre-order the device.

"Get Ready" let users choose the color and capacity of the device, plus specify carrier and finance details. Apple ran this from October 12 until late on October 15.

If you didn't go through this process, you may well find that the iPhone Duo sells out before you reach that "Buy" button. As well as the normal high demand for a new iPhone, it's believed that there will be lower stocks than normal.

However, Apple reserves stock for its Apple Stores. Those will be selling, and perhaps most importantly demonstrating, the iPhone Duo from October 23.

items.title: Apple's Minions research turns idle Mac GPUs into a virtual GPU cloud
items.content_html:
Apple has detailed a new system, called Minions, that uses the idle GPUs found in Apple Silicon Macs to create a virtual GPU cloud that combines untapped processing power to chew through complex AI workloads.

Described by Apple as a dynamic virtual GPU cloud that "aggregates idle Apple Silicon GPUs" across Macs, Minions can aid teams that need to work with large-scale machine learning inference workloads. Apple's researchers have been using Minions in-house already.

The theory is a simple one. Macs have powerful GPUs that spend most of their time idle, especially during everyday computing tasks.

Minions is designed to leverage the GPU processing power that isn't being used, turning otherwise underused Macs into a cluster of AI-ready machines.

Both the Mac mini and Mac Studio support clustering via the Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) system using Thunderbolt 5 connections. These high-bandwidth cables allow compute and memory to be combined from multiple machines, putting them to work on a single workload.

Minions is an expansion of that concept.

Apple's documentation explains that there are four key components required for Minions to function.

First, a Minions Server acts as the central coordinator, handling all of the requests via a web-based interface and APIs. Once a job has been handed to the Minions Server, everything is handed off and queued into a PostgreSQL metadata store.

Minion Executors run on the macOS devices whose GPU cycles are to be harvested for the Minions system. These Executors execute subtasks locally using the Apple Silicon GPUs and then write their results to storage.

If a failure occurs, such as during a connectivity failure or power loss, the Minion Watchdog re-queues the failed job for execution on another machine.

The whole process is fed back into a dashboard for real-time monitoring.

Apple argues that, in its experience, Minion has proven that macOS devices can be turned into a distributed GPU inference platform when needed.

Apple also says that, in its testing, some inference jobs that previously took more than 10 hours have been slashed to mere minutes. And all without the need for additional infrastructure and with an easy path to increased scale.

When that might be needed will differ from one use case to the next. But it's easy to imagine an office full of Macs having their GPU cycles harvested in this way, as the "Minions" method does not appear to require Thunderbolt.

For businesses, the benefits of something like Minions are obvious. Slashing processing time without having to buy additional hardware is always a plus, especially as prices continue to skyrocket.

Some businesses may also see this as a good reason to buy Apple devices come refresh time. Something Apple will surely encourage.

items.title: Joswiak: Siri AI is for everyday, not the AI 'lunatic fringe'
items.content_html:
Apple Intelligence isn't made to be like Claude, Grok, or other AI tools that the Silicon Valley "lunatic fringe" praise, says Greg Joswiak, it's built to help regular users.

Apple has long been criticized for being behind on AI with Apple Intelligence, although the improved Siri AI has answered many complaints. But speaking to Time magazine, Apple's senior vice president of worldwide marketing, Greg Joswiak, said that the company is not making AI for fans of the technology.

"We love them, and they can use it too, but that's not our target," he said. "It's how to make it better for everyday people."

Joswiak says he sees the purpose of Siri AI to be useful for ordinary people. He does not believe that Apple should aim at impressing the "lunatic fringe" of AI super fans.

That does raise the issue of whether those fans will abandon Apple, and whether that's a problem.

"We don't feel threatened," said Joswiak. "The fact that we can do the integration that we can means we can create just a better experience than anybody else."

Joswiak was speaking to Time for its cover story about the new Apple CEO, John Ternus. That concentrates on how Ternus spent 15 years working on what would become the iPhone Duo.

He and Joswiak have previously talked about some of that process, and particularly about keeping the design secret.

The iPhone Duo was announced on September 9, 2026. Pre-orders for it begin on October 16, and shipping starts on October 23.

items.title: Devil is in the details: Tidbits from our time trying HomeView
items.content_html:
We've learned a few finicky details from Apple's HomeView launch, including how the live security camera tiles work, how photo albums are displayed, and how to mount the display where a light switch used to be.

Apple introduced HomeView on October 13, but some of its smaller features deserve a closer look. Beyond the hardware and Siri AI features covered in our HomeView hands-on, details from the launch demonstrations reveal more about how the device works around the house.

AppleInsider's Andrew O'Hara got hands-on time with HomeView during Apple's launch event. His demonstrations revealed several smaller details about how the display handles security cameras, shared photos, recipes, and smart home controls.

From its animated faces to recipe management and security cameras, there's quite a bit packed into Apple's seven-inch display.

The Home Camera face can display up to nine simultaneous live video feeds instead of static camera snapshots. Owners can monitor multiple rooms, entrances, or outdoor areas without switching between individual cameras.

During Apple's demonstrations, the feeds were responsive with little noticeable delay. It was a controlled environment, though, so we'll have to see whether that performance holds up with different home networks and camera configurations.

Although many of the new Apple Home Collection accessories support Matter, the cameras don't use the standard, at least for now.

Apple representatives explained to us that the current Matter camera specification has shortcomings involving reliability and security. Matter has supported cameras since version 1.5, but Apple has chosen a different approach for its new models.

HomeView's Photos face isn't limited to pictures stored in someone's personal library. It also supports shared albums, allowing other people to contribute photos that can appear on the display.

For example, someone could give HomeView to a parent or grandparent, select a shared album, and continue adding pictures from their own iPhone. The recipient wouldn't need to manually transfer each new photo to the display.

HomeView can replace a dedicated digital photo frame, especially for families who already use iCloud Shared Albums. Owners also get smart home controls and other features without needing a separate device on the counter.

Some of HomeView's faces do more than display a clock or decorative animation. The Flow face, borrowed from Apple Watch, uses HomeView's camera to respond to movement around the room.

On Apple Watch, Flow reacts to movement of the wearer's wrist. HomeView adapts that idea to a stationary display, changing the animation as people move nearby.

Another face, called Fade, takes inspiration from a sundial. Its clock numerals gradually fade in and out depending on the time, changing the display's appearance throughout the day.

Both faces give HomeView something to show when nobody is actively using its smart home controls.

HomeView's recipe features aren't restricted to content from Apple News. Recipes found through Safari can also be opened in the device's cooking interface, giving owners access to instructions from websites they already use.

Supported recipes appear as step-by-step instructions, and Siri can advance to the next step with a voice command. Cooks can follow along without touching the display with messy hands.

Recipes can also be pinned for future use, making it easier to return to favorite dishes without searching for the original website again.

For now, Safari and Apple News are the supported routes for bringing recipes into HomeView. Dedicated integrations with third-party recipe apps remain a separate question.

We've been speculating about this since the debut. HomeView's wall-mounted model doesn't necessarily need a visible power cable.

With the Schneider Home Power Mount AC Wired accessory, it can connect directly to household electrical wiring through a standard single-gang wall box.

HomeView can be installed where a conventional light switch previously sat, provided the wiring is suitable.

A $79.95 mount supplies continuous power over USB-C and keeps the connection hidden behind the display. It also means HomeView can serve as a permanent control panel near an entrance, where someone would normally reach for a light switch.

There are some electrical considerations, however. Existing switch wiring isn't automatically suitable for powering HomeView, and replacing a switch also requires accounting for the lighting circuit it previously controlled.

Apple recommends a licensed electrician for the hardwired mount. We're less certain about that.

For homes with suitable wiring, the result could be a cleaner installation than mounting a tablet and running a charging cable down the wall.

HomeView starts at $299, with both tabletop and wall-mounted models available to preorder ahead of the November 13 release. The wall-mounted version requires a separate mounting accessory, but we're looking forward to what the 3D printing community cranks out.

The launch demonstrations provide an early look at how these features work, but their everyday usefulness will depend on how well HomeView performs once it's installed in actual homes.

items.title: Ternus spent 15 years planning the iPhone Duo
items.content_html:
New CEO John Ternus believes Apple should get designs right rather than launch early or emulate rivals, and the iPhone Duo is an example of that.

Ternus was named as Tim Cook's successor in April 2026, around 25 years after he first joined the company. But after just 10 years, he was already involved in what would become the iPhone Duo.

Speaking to Time magazine, he said that he and five fellow engineers had even filed a patent for foldable devices in 2011. "It felt clear that we were going to eventually get to a place where OLED displays were going to be flexible."

Before that led to the launch of the iPhone Duo, though, Samsung and many other rivals beat Apple to market. Yet Ternus wasn't concerned, saying that the "other examples in the world felt kind of cheap and crappy."

This determination to just get it right first is backed up by Richard Dinh, Apple's vice president of product design, who told the publication that Apple could have launched sooner.

While Dinh would not say when it could have brought out a foldable iPhone, he does say that he specifically talked with Ternus about it because of how rivals were already launching. Apple had a foldable with a top surface similar to those of rivals, and while he says it had flaws, Dinh thought it might be good enough.

iPhone Duo's final glass layers

"[But Ternus] was like, 'Look, Rich, you'll know when it's the right thing,'" said Dinh. "And that gave us the confidence to really push the boundaries on innovation and manufacturing, and fly worldwide to connect our suppliers together and come up with the nanotexture [surface]."

It may take its time entering new markets, and Apple has a reputation for wanting to build everything itself, but Ternus doesn't agree with that. Nor does he think everything Apple does works right away.

For instance, he says that he used Screen Time with his own children and found it to be "good but not great." Naturally, he says now that the updates are better.

"[We wanted] to build tools that make that really easy for parents," he continued. "And I think we've done just that."

As for owning the whole stack from software down to every hardware component, Ternus believes in controlling what you can control. "There's not really a goal that we have to make every single thing in a product," he says. "We make the things where we can really bring differentiation."

"You can't do everything," he stresses. "So we kind of try to constrain ourselves to the stuff that matters most — and then put all of our effort into those things."

Apple's new Siri AI aside, there has been a perception that one of the things the company can't do is compete with its rivals in AI. Ternus didn't directly address that, but repeats Apple's position that with its privacy and ecosystem, it has an advantage.

"Everything in your life is on your phone," he says. "With Siri AI, you can leverage all that information to do things, learn things, and figure out things in a way that nobody else can do."

Ternus also believes in the longevity of the iPhone and hardware in general, and not in everybody talking to AI to accomplish everything.

"People want physical things," he says. "They want to talk, to see images of loved ones, to take pictures."

"So I don't see a scenario where all of a sudden, our devices disappear and we don't have a need for an iPhone," he concludes.

Ternus has this long history with Apple hardware, but now that he's CEO, he has to deal with so much more. And that includes politics.

John Ternus (left) and his predecessor Tim Cook - image credit: Apple.

Apple has recently been criticized for wanting to buy processors and memory from Chinese manufacturers. Ternus sticks by that, though, arguing that the "constraints in memory are absolutely a crisis."

"So our fundamental belief is that all options should be on the table," he says.

Perhaps more contentiously, his predecessor was robustly criticized for his dealings with Trump, from personally donating to the inauguration, and for presenting him with a random trophy.

Ternus has now met with members of the current administration. He says he's done this to "make sure we're kind of working through things together."

There were no more details, but Ternus also pointed to how Tim Cook is staying on at the company as Executive Chairman. "He has great relationships and loves Apple," says Ternus, "so wherever he can help, he is happy to help."

items.title: Touch-screen MacBook Pro will be unveiled on October 28
items.content_html:
Apple is reportedly preparing an October 28 launch for a series of iPad and Mac releases, ranging from the OLED touch-screen MacBook Pro to a new iPad mini.

Following its unveiling of the HomeView on October 12, 2026 with briefings and videos rather than an event, Apple is now expected to do the same again. According to Bloomberg, an extensive all-day press briefing is now scheduled for Wednesday, October 28.

Apple is now inviting some media to an all-day product launch experience on Oct. 28 in Los Angeles. This is for the touch-screen MacBooks, iPad mini, M6 Macs.

This second launch has been rumored for some time, and believed to center on the expected OLED touch-screen MacBook Pro. There has also been speculation that it might feature a mixture of Mac and iPad launches.

Specifically, an updated iPad mini with an OLED screen has been predicted. Rumors claim that it will have an 8.4-inch LTPS rear panel with hybrid OLED, but also a 60Hz refresh rate and so no ProMotion.

The new claim that the October 28 unveiling will include M6 Macs, plural, could mean the 14-inch MacBook Pro and 16-inch MacBook Pro, but most likely refers to the iMac. It's now two years since the iMac was updated, and previous reports have claimed that an M6 version would be released before the end of 2026.

It could be quite close to the end of the year, though. If an M6 iMac is launched on October 28, it's unlikely that it will be shipping that day.

Instead, it's much more likely that pre-orders will open in early November, with shipping between the middle and the end of the month. Apple will presumably want the earliest date possible, as an iMac could be a big seller for the holiday season.

The new HomeView could well be the same. That would help Apple's earnings, as this year, it does not have a new base iPhone in its lineup.

items.title: iPhone Duo delivery dates stabilize on late January deliveries for all models
items.content_html:
If you missed out on getting your iPhone Duo Friday morning, you likely won't see yours show up until early 2027. At least is isn't getting worse anymore.

On Friday, Apple opened preorders for the iPhone Duo, its first foldable. Announced in September, the buzz following the event left little doubt that it would be an immediate hit.

And that certainly seems to be the case. The iPhone Duo sold out almost immediately, with dates slipping into late November and early December within moments of preorders opening.

As of Friday afternoon, the iPhone Duo dates have slipped into late January. That holds regardless of storage size or color, suggesting that demand is equal across configuration or supply numbers are low.

iPhone Duo delivery dates have been pushed into January

Apple never states how many devices it has made ready for sale on day one, but the shipping dates normally provide a clue as to whether a model is a hit.

Carriers had stock until later in the process. AT&T and Verizon had same-week delivery until about noon. Best Buy had a two-week shipment for most models as late as 2PM ET on October 16.

Supply from the carriers seems to fluctuate, though, and they tend to over-promise and under-deliver. Apple is more conservative with under-promising and shipping early, in most cases

For those who want to try their luck in brick-and-mortar stores, the iPhone Duo will be available to purchase in-store on October 23. You should expect increased crowd sizes and lines, though, and going to an Apple Store does not mean you'll leave with an iPhone Duo, either.

items.title: iPhone Duo has uncompromised performance, same as iPhone 18 Pro
items.content_html:
If the first Geekbench 7 figures for the iPhone Duo are legit, the A20 Pro processor hasn't been slowed down by the foldable's design choices.

It's not be a huge surprise that two iPhones with the same A20 Pro processor would show at least similar benchmark results. However, the processor is just part of the whole system, and the iPhone 18 Pro has room for a larger vapor chamber cooling system.

As first spotted by NotebookCheck, what the first Geekbench 7 results show, though, is that the performance of the iPhone Duo has not been materially affected by its thin and folding design.

The iPhone Duo even fractionally beats the iPhone 18 Pro in Geekbench 7's single-core tests. It's well within testing error margins, though, as iPhone Duo scores 3,986 compared to the iPhone 18 Pro's 3,980.

Longer bars are better, but good luck being able to see the difference between these two.

But even so, the figure demonstrates that the iPhone Duo will feel as fast as the iPhone 18 Pro in general use. Single-core tests show how the phone works for opening apps, browsing, and so on.

With multi-core performance, the story is the same. The iPhone Duo scores 11,067, while the iPhone 18 Pro gets 11,540. This too is well within the margin of error, and an insignificant difference.

There's a more pronounced difference in multi-core test scores, although the iPhone Duo is still at the heels of the iPhone 18 Pro.

Nonetheless, the iPhone Duo's multi-core score is still considerably higher than the iPhone 17 Pro. That model with an A19 Pro processor scored 9,909 in this test.

The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are available now. Pre-orders for the iPhone Duo begin on October 16, and shipping is from October 23.

items.title: Apple HomeView hands on: So many questions, but I like it
items.content_html:
At Apple's NYC experience, I got an early look at HomeView, its new smart home display. I still have unanswered questions but my early take is that I like it. A lot.

Most of you have seen the general rundown on the hardware. It's a 7-inch Liquid Retina display, perched atop a speaker base or mounted to a wall that you can control with your voice or touch.

It has Siri AI built-in to operate your smart home, answer questions, find your lost Apple TV 4K Siri Remote, or otherwise control it. There's a built-in camera that can recognize up to six distinct users to load personal information, such as message history or calendars.

The device ships with a series of Apple apps such as Calendar, Safari, Music, and more. Additional apps are supported via your iPhone, like Apple TV.

My first impression was how much I loved the look of it. It's small. Cute even.

HomeView can get very dark, making it great for sitting next to your bed

The display feels just the right size to easily fit onto a night stand, desk, or kitchen counter without being too big. It's a bright display, too, looking crisp and sharp from anywhere, even in the well-lit demo areas.

I love the wealth of faces, as Apple calls them, that it designed for the HomeView. Some of these are entirely new, while others are borrowed from the Apple TV and Apple Watch.

The Flow face reacts to your movements

The Flow face on Apple Watch reacts to your wrist movements, while on the HomeView, it reacts to your movements in the room. One face looks like a sundial, fading the numerals in and out of view over time.

HomeView showing the Snoopy face that reacts to time, the calendar, and the weather.

I've always been a fan of the Snoopy face, and even if I want to put the data-heavy modular face in the kitchen, I fret my children are going to be insistent here. The Snoopy one still animates and takes cues from the calendar and weather, pulling out an umbrella when it's raining.

Not to dwell too much on the idle faces here, but I think the Photos face is also another winner. You can use a shared photo album for this, so if another family member outside the house has a HomeView, it's effortless to contribute new photos to their device.

HomeView sitting on a kitchen counter

I know multiple people who use digital photo frames for this exact reason and Apple easily created a more seamless version that also has a bunch of other features.

These faces all looked very polished and useful. It's going to be hard to decide whether to go with usable controls or gorgeous clock faces.

As I went through the demo home, there were a lot of those little "oh, I love that!" moments the more I used HomeView.

Using HandOff to send over a Recipe in Safari to HomeView

Using HandOff to transfer a recipe into a helpful cooking view is genuinely useful and you can use Siri to move step to step hands-free. It also doesn't require any app or special Apple News link — just a recipe in Safari that can be pinned for future use.

Mirror mode on HomeView with an edge ring light

The mirror was also quite clever. When you get ready for the day, you can open the mirror app to see yourself. HomeView has a closeup view where you can clearly see your face, or you can zoom out for a full-body look.

If it's dark, you can turn on the edge ring light. A similar lighting feature is also available on the Mac.

Beyond the basic uses of the HomeView, what I was here for was the smart home aspect. I desperately want an always-on smart display to control my Apple Home devices and thus far, that functionality has been limited to almost every other ecosystem.

Live camera feed on HomeView

You can do this with an iPad, but it's not the same. There's no multi-user support, ideal dashboard view, perfect mounting option, and I'd also miss intercom and hub functionality.

I specifically wanted a streamlined device that was designed from the beginning to be a smart display, and not a tablet. That's what we got with HomeView.

Someone ringing the doorbell which then shows on HomeView

The camera feed face is perfect to see real-time live camera streams from your home and the modular face lets you choose exactly what accessories you want to prioritize as always available.

Apple has all-new animations and styles for each of the interactions, like controlling the thermostat or lights. They were designed for this screen size and will be easy for anyone to understand and use.

I think one of the most popular uses for HomeView will be replacing your in-wall light switches. This is possible with the AC hardwire mount and something a lot of savvy users will be able to do themselves.

Especially wall mounted, the HomeView is a great place to put your smart home controls

You tie off your lights to be always-on and swap the "dumb" bulb for a smart bulb and you're good to go. I think that's exactly what I'd like to do.

For as bullish as I am on HomeView, I do think there is a lot to come. This, in many ways, feels like Apple's early version of the Apple Watch.

I think having some system-wide gesture would prove useful, instead of tucked away as an accessibility setting. I'd love a gesture that, similar to the double-tap on Apple Watch, could pause a track, move to the next step in a recipe, or end a FaceTime call.

Various apps available on HomeView

It's also not unjustified to ask for more app integrations. I understand Apple's preferred method of interaction is largely voice with simple tasks, but that shouldn't entirely limit HomeView to this awkward CarPlay scenario that only will allow audio and video apps.

We'll have to wait closer to launch, but I'm curious about how widgets will work. The demo units only had Apple's stock apps installed so there wasn't an opportunity to try any CarPlay streaming apps or widgets.

It would be great to have the Matic robovac app on there, which works with Apple Home, but has further cleaning customization within its own app. In the Matic app, I can change the room cleaning order or direct it to a spill.

Recipe apps like Crouton, NYT Cooking, or Paprika seem to be natural fits too. Apple's recipe implementation looks great, but the only recipes you can load are via Safari.

The guided recipe experience on HomeView

I do think that much of this will come down the line, but it does highlight some of the holes in the initial implementation. The good news is the hardware is there and looks gorgeous.

Hopefully we see next steps at WWDC in June. Fingers crossed for a proper pipeline for more third-party integrations.

Right now, I plan on buying at least three HomeViews for my home. Originally, I thought I'd only end up with one in the kitchen.

I want one bedside, which is possible, in part, because of the special low-light mode that lets the display get super dim. This would be a great dashboard to control all the individual smart lights in our room, while also being able to see any security cameras.

We already were planning on putting a HomePod mini in the room. For $150 more, we can get a HomeView with far more utility.

Of course there will be a kitchen one for family use. I'm sure it will be used constantly for cooking, watching YouTube, checking the shared family calendar, or FaceTime calls.

My studio absolutely needs one. I could tie this into all my different scenes for working, filming, or podcasting, plus it would be physical controls for my smart shades.

As HomeView evolves, and we even see more third-party customizations and accessories, this could go further. I'm particularly interested if anyone makes an articulating arm that would allow one to be mounted on my desk.

It's a new device category and admittedly somewhat limited out of the box, but I think the potential is there and I'm very excited to finally start using it. After more than five years of rumors, HomeView is finally here.

items.title: OpenAI cries foul, says Apple stole secrets from it in 2026
items.content_html:
In a new filing, OpenAI claims that it too was victimized by confidential information theft, and implies that Apple's HomeView was somehow influenced by that theft.

Without much detail, OpenAI says that during the forensic investigation that is required by Apple's trade secret theft lawsuit, it discovered trade theft by Apple. In a filing on Wednesday, the company vaguely says that the thief joined OpenAI from Apple, worked at OpenAI for six months, then returned to Apple.

When the alleged thief returned to Apple, they brought with them details of one OpenAI hardware device stashed away in personal accounts. Furthermore, the documents include specific images, engineering info, supplier information, manufacturing data, and standards for cosmetic finishes and sealants.

In short, OpenAI is accusing this employee, who returned to work at Apple in June 2026, of the same thing that Apple alleges. And, in the filing, OpenAI is drawing a spurious and strange parallel to the HomeView, which has been in development for at least three years that we are aware of.

"That presentation appears to have happened months ago," The filing says. "Armed with that information, Apple is making a new push into AI-enabled products."

OpenAI claims that the employee made presentations about product plans to Apple's vice president of operations in Asia. The company also says that it has raised this issue with Apple.

Apple reportedly never responded. However, it has denied that the theft or briefing happened, and says there is no evidence surrounding the incident that the company holds.

In a statement to Reuters on Wednesday, Apple says that it has "policies and procedures in place to ensure new employees do not use confidential information" from OpenAI, or any other company.

We could not identify the alleged thief. The filing does not say who it is, which in itself is unusual.

Apple alleges that its former employees, Tang Yew Tan and Chang Liu, stole the company's trade secrets through iCloud exploits. They then used that information to benefit OpenAI in an attempt to benefit OpenAI.

According to Apple, the two stole information by continuing to use work-issued devices and services after leaving the company. The two allegedly also abused bugs, emailed themselves supplier information, and instructed Apple employees interviewing with OpenAI to bring unreleased Apple hardware with them.

As a result, Apple filed a lawsuit against its former employees and against OpenAI in July 2026.

Naturally, OpenAI denied the accusations, and said that they had procedures to prevent this kind of thing, and to stop leaks like they are alleging as well.

There has been a considerable amount of legal drama in the last five months, and there will be much more going forward up to and including the trial, which has not been scheduled yet. However, on Tuesday, Judge Edward Davila partly granted Apple's requests for relevant OpenAI information about the employees in question.

items.title: Apple's $1,499 iPhone Duo repair cost is a strong argument for AppleCare
items.content_html:
After viewing the repair costs on Apple's first foldable, we've got a bit of advice for you: go ahead and add AppleCare to your cart right now.

Apple has released the uninsured repair costs for the iPhone Duo, and they aren't for the faint of heart. Depending on what damage your phone takes, you could pay 75% of the retail value to get it fixed.

Here's what it costs to repair an iPhone Duo, assuming you don't have insurance through your carrier or AppleCare.

The "other damage" category, which typically denotes damage that can't be replaced with a simple component swap, costs nearly $1,500. That's 75% of the $1,999 price tag, assuming you purchased a base-model iPhone Duo.

If you have AppleCare, the prices are significantly lower. Here's what you can expect to pay.

For other damage, AppleCare drops the cost by $1,400, which is roughly 93% cheaper. If nothing else, it's a poignant reminder that investing in a good insurance plan, like AppleCare, can save you a lot of money.

items.title: Regular iPhone 18 nears production in large quanties, says obvious leak
items.content_html:
Sometimes you don't need inside sources to be a "leaker," you just need a calendar. Right on cue, a leaker is claiming that the iPhone 18 will shortly be produced en masse.

Just as was rumored for a year, Apple split its 2026 iPhone launch in two. The second wave of iPhones features the base iPhone 18 and is expected in spring 2027.

Now leaker Fixed Focus Digital has claimed on the Chinese social media platform Weibo that this model will enter mass manufacturing presently.

"The standard version of [iPhone] 18 is scheduled for production," says the leaker (in machine translation), "and judging by the inventory levels, the stockpile is quite substantial."

It would be. In previous years, it has always been the case that it's the Pro and Pro Max models of the iPhone that are the big sellers from launch up to Christmas. Then the tide shifts in February or so, and the base or regular model becomes the top seller.

This time there is a question over whether buyers who would normally have gone for the base model may have bought the iPhone 18 Pro instead. But it's unlikely to have been a significant percentage, and so Apple can reasonably forecast similar volumes for the iPhone 18 as for the iPhone 17.

Those volumes are huge, too, so obviously the stockpile of components will be large. Then in order to have the iPhone 18 ready for sale in spring 2027, production must start months ahead.

So a report saying that iPhone 18 production is to begin in November and there will be substantial numbers made, is not startling.

But at least it presumably means that manufacturing is on schedule for the new base iPhone.

Note that Fixed Focus Digital has a mixed track record, but they were correct when they said that rumors of an iPhone Duo delay were false.

items.title: Precision Finding on the new Siri Remote comes with an unexpected catch
items.content_html:
Apple's new Siri Remote adds Precision Finding, but the feature won't work with iPhone 15 or iPhone 16 models, as Apple is using a new Bluetooth-based technology.

Introduced alongside the fourth-generation Apple TV, the updated remote adds more precise location guidance through Find My and a built-in tone inducer that can play a sound when the remote goes missing.

However, Apple's compatibility requirements exclude several relatively recent iPhones, including models that already support advanced location tracking with other Apple accessories.

According to Apple's footnotes, Precision Finding requires an iPhone Duo, iPhone Air, or iPhone 17 or later, excluding the iPhone 17e. Compatible iPhones must run the latest version of iOS, and availability varies by region.

The restriction is particularly notable because the iPhone 15 lineup and most iPhone 16 models already feature Apple's second-generation Ultra Wideband chip. Those iPhones support expanded Precision Finding with the AirTag 2, but they can't use the new Siri Remote's Precision Finding feature.

The reason is that Apple isn't using Ultra Wideband as with AirTag and AirPods. Instead, it's using a new feature recently added to the Bluetooth spec.

In Bluetooth 6, there is a new part of the spec called Channel Sounding, which is likely what Apple is utilizing. Channel Sounding has centimeter-level precision combining Phase-Based Ranging (PBR) and Round-Trip Timing (RTT).

PBR measures the distance in radio signal phases across multiple frequencies and RTT times how long the signals take to go between devices. Together, they mimic UWB functionality at a lower cost as it doesn't require dedicated hardware.

Owners of older iPhones aren't entirely out of options. Since iOS 17, Apple's existing remote finder has helped users locate second-generation and newer Siri Remotes using proximity indicators that show whether they're getting closer to or farther from the device.

Precision Finding provides more detailed location guidance, while the ability to play a sound is exclusive to the fourth-generation Siri Remote. The new Siri Remote is compatible with Apple TV HD and every Apple TV 4K generation, and Apple will sell it separately.

Owners of older Apple TV hardware can therefore upgrade their remote without purchasing the new $299 Apple TV 4K. The fourth-generation Apple TV 4K is available for preorder starting October 13, with availability beginning November 13.

items.title: Withings wants you to pay $100 to sync data with Apple Health
items.content_html:
Withings has introduced an Apple Health Sync paywall, requiring all new users to pay $99.99 each year to see their weight within Apple's default Health app.

Withings is a French company known for its smart scales, some of which analyze more than 60 biomarkers, while also offering built-in electrodes and a rechargeable battery. The company also touted its dedicated Withings app, as well as its products' integration with Apple Health.

As it turns out, however, that Apple Health integration will come at a great cost to new users. As noted by a user of the Withings forum, accounts created after October 13, 2026, are required to have a $99 Withings+ subscription to sync their scale data with Apple Health. The feature will remain free for existing Withings users.

"Taking a fundamental feature that has always been free and locking it behind a paywall for new users is an obvious cash grab," says the user. They also claim that writing data to Apple Health using HealthKit on an iPhone doesn't require server-side processing, AI agents, or any other potential costs for Withings.

According to the Withings forum user, the company justified this seemingly arbitrarily imposed paywall with "privacy measures" and an "AI connector." In the comments, Withings itself confirmed the decision to charge for Apple Health syncing via the Withings+ subscription.

In the rather vague statement, Withings said that its "mission hasn't changed" and that Withings+ "funds the services" around user data. The company did not specify exactly what services the subscription actually funds.

In an attempt to appease upset users, Withings also noted that some basic features would remain free. It explained that every user can "export their full history as CSV or PDF at any time, keep importing data from other apps, and share data with their doctor through HealthLink and PDF reports."

Withings users, meanwhile, remain largely unconvinced and unsatisfied, calling the decision "absolutely terrible" and "awful," among other things. This sentiment is understandable, given that a free feature has found itself behind a seemingly arbitrary paywall.

Worse yet, while a product like the $599.95 Withings BodyScan 2 requires a subscription to sync your data with Apple Health, other scales do it for free. For instance, the iHealth Nexus Pro smart scale, priced at a whole $30, syncs data with its iHealth app and with Apple Health at no additional cost.

The iHealth Nexus Pro is simply an illustrative example, and there are likely many more scales with free Apple Health syncing available on online marketplaces. For something as basic as a scale, there's little reason to opt for a yearly subscription, unless specific medical or dietary needs are part of the equation.

items.title: New in iOS 27.2 beta 4: Apple Health, Apple Music changes
items.content_html:
While iOS 27.2 beta 4 brought a new look for Apple Music and a reference to a new HomePod setting, it also curiously removed an upcoming Apple Health upgrade. Here's what you need to know.

On Tuesday, shortly after unveiling its HomeView and other smart home products, Apple deployed the fourth developer beta of iOS 27.2. The beta software update bears the build number 24B5110a, up from 24B5099f.

In a particularly noticeable visual change, iOS 27.2 beta 4 removes all color from the Apple Music icon. Now, it's just a black musical note on a white background, or inverted in dark mode, rather than the white and red look the icon has used since iOS 14.

Though it might seem like an unusual stylistic change for Apple to make, it's not the first time the company has altered the color scheme of the Apple Music icon. Before the now-replaced orange color, the Apple Music icon on iOS 8.4 through iOS 13 had a multi-colored note against a white background.

It remains to be seen whether the new black-and-white Apple Music icon will make it to the release version of iOS 27.2, especially as Apple may have delayed another feature. The fourth developer beta of iOS 27.2 outright lacks the redesigned Apple Health app seen in previous beta builds.

The app itself features new AI-powered summaries and suggestions, along with layout changes, among other things. It's expected to arrive with iOS 27.2, though Tuesday's developer beta suggests Apple might have other plans regarding when to release it.

In place of the revamped Apple Health app is a message saying the overhaul is "coming later this year." Data on devices running the latest iOS 27.2 beta remains viewable in the Settings app, though.

Additionally, iOS 27.2 beta 4 has a new setting for HomePods. The new slider is labeled Lock Controls. "When Lock Controls is enabled, touch interactions for touch, touch and hold, and volume are disabled," reads the description.

Overall, the fourth developer beta of iOS 27.2 is a relatively minor update, offering virtually nothing beyond the black-and-white Apple Music icon. Depending on what Apple does with its redesigned Health app, the iOS 27.2 update could prove to be less impressive than initially expected.
